entities.summary:
Gaius Aquillius Florus was one of the two consuls of the Roman Republic in 259 BCE, and his consular colleague was Lucius Cornelius Scipio. Together they fought in the ongoing First Punic War, which lasted from 264 to 241 BCE and saw the Roman Republic clash with Carthage. This conflict was a defining moment in the struggle for Mediterranean supremacy, pitting the expanding Roman state against the powerful Carthaginian Empire. The war's outcome was a decisive Roman victory, securing the island of Sicily and Corsica, and paving the way for Rome's future expansion. Florus's own legacy is largely overshadowed by that of his more famous colleague Scipio, but his consular colleague was an important figure in Roman politics and a skilled military commander.

Gaius Aquillius Florus was born in 320 BCE, in the Roman province of Picenum, in what is now modern-day Italy. He was a member of the Roman aristocracy and a prominent figure in the Roman Republic, serving as a consul in 259 BCE and a quaestor in 257 BCE. Florus's military campaigns took him to Sicily, where he fought alongside Scipio against the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca. Florus's own military tactics were notable for their innovative use of cavalry and his ability to adapt to changing circumstances on the battlefield. Despite his successes, Florus's career was marked by controversy and personal scandals, which ultimately led to his downfall.
